```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
prev <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/items_prevalence.csv", verbose = FALSE)
tet  <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/items_tetrachoric.csv", verbose = FALSE)
eig  <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/efa_eigen.csv", verbose = FALSE)
load <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/efa_loadings.csv", verbose = FALSE)
phi  <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/efa_factor_corr.csv", verbose = FALSE)
cfa  <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/cfa_fit.csv", verbose = FALSE)
rel  <- datawizard::data_read("_model-outputs/scale_reliability.csv", verbose = FALSE)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
num <- function(x, d = 2) gsub("-", "−", formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f"), fixed = TRUE)
n_resp <- prev$n_respondents[1]

scale_order <- c("cosmopolitan", "utilitarian", "communitarian", "libertarian")
item_order  <- prev |> datawizard::data_modify(scale = factor(scale, scale_order)) |> datawizard::data_arrange("scale") |> dplyr::pull(item)
tet_r <- function(a, b) tet$tetrachoric[tet$item == a & tet$with == b]

l4 <- load |> datawizard::data_filter(solution == "4-factor")
l2 <- load |> datawizard::data_filter(solution == "2-factor")
ld <- function(item, f, sol = l4) sol[[f]][sol$item == item]
phi4 <- phi |> datawizard::data_filter(solution == "4-factor")
phi2 <- phi |> datawizard::data_filter(solution == "2-factor")
fit <- function(m, col) cfa[[col]][cfa$model == m]
alpha <- function(s) rel$ordinal_alpha[rel$scale == s]
# the caption of the loadings table, built here because a colon inside a YAML
# !expr string is read as a mapping
# section 9: the outcome decisions of the curve, from the files written by the course
# pipeline; every fit there is on country-year aggregates
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
neg <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve_negative.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>

devs <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "construction")
dev_rows <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
pp <- \(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(x * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
below_sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports & d$sig)
fk <- \(ax, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == ax]
dv <- \(op, col) devs[[col]][devs$option == op]
# the reproduced specification, with the frame set and the item set left free
at_ref <- \(d) d |>
  dplyr::filter(predictor == "unemp", copredictor == "none", estimator == "fe_twoway",
         noop == "zero", cell_weight == "unweighted", measure == "wb_nat", pred_form == "raw")
r_at <- \(d, out, items = "all") at_ref(d) |>
  dplyr::filter(outcome == out, item_set == items) |>
  dplyr::pull(r_ca)
count_ref <- at_ref(dev_rows) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(axis == "construction", option == "count", outcome == "mcosmo", item_set == "all")
# cell means at the standard measurement settings, share and count side by side
cell_wide <- datawizard::data_read("../data/teney_panel_measurement.csv", verbose = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(item_set == "all", noop == "zero", cell_weight == "unweighted",
         outcome %in% c("mcosmo", "mpos", "mneg")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = c(cntry, year), names_from = c(construction, outcome),
              values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::mutate(total = count_mpos + count_mneg,
         pos_within = share_mpos - mean(share_mpos),
         neg_within = (1 - share_mneg) - mean(1 - share_mneg), .by = cntry)

cap_efa4 <- sprintf("The four-factor exploratory solution (minimum residual, oblimin rotation), accounting for %.1f%% of the variance in the items. Loadings under 0.30 are blank. Communality is the share of the variance of an item that the four factors reproduce together. Factor correlations: 1 with 4, %.2f; 2 with 3, %.2f; every positive factor with every negative one between %s and %s.", 100 * mean(l4$communality), phi4$F4[phi4$factor == "F1"], phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F2"], num(min(phi4$F2[phi4$factor == "F1"], phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F1"], phi4$F2[phi4$factor == "F4"], phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F4"])), num(max(phi4$F2[phi4$factor == "F1"], phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F1"], phi4$F2[phi4$factor == "F4"], phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F4"])))

# sections 10 and 11: the respondents who mention nothing, from the files of the
# course panel and the curve, with percentages through pp(), which rounds halves
# up as the specification menu does
cy  <- datawizard::data_read("../data/europeanisation_cy.csv", verbose = FALSE)
pw  <- datawizard::data_read("../data/teney_panel_weights.csv", verbose = FALSE)
me  <- datawizard::data_read("../data/teney_panel_measurement.csv", verbose = FALSE)
mi  <- datawizard::data_read("../data/spec_grid_mi.csv", verbose = FALSE)
dg  <- datawizard::data_read("../data/mi_diagnostics.csv", verbose = FALSE)
noop_devs <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "noop")
noop_rows <- dev_rows |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "noop")

n_all  <- sum(pw$n_cy); n_noop <- sum(pw$n_noop)
n_dk <- sum(pw$n_dk); n_oth <- sum(pw$n_other); n_bl <- sum(pw$n_blank)
noop_cy <- cy |> dplyr::inner_join(pw |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("cntry", "year", "noop_rate")), by = c("cntry", "year"))
r_noop_unemp <- cor(noop_cy$noop_rate, noop_cy$unemp)
r_noop_cosmo <- cor(noop_cy$noop_rate, noop_cy$mcosmo)
by_c <- pw |> dplyr::summarise(rate = mean(noop_rate), .by = cntry) |> datawizard::data_arrange("-rate")

# the no-opinion rate within countries, net of the common yearly movement
m_noop <- fixest::feols(noop_rate ~ unemp | cntry + year, data = noop_cy, vcov = "iid")
noop_b <- coef(m_noop)[["unemp"]]
noop_t <- fixest::coeftable(m_noop)["unemp", "t value"]
noop_t_cl <- fixest::coeftable(m_noop, vcov = ~cntry)["unemp", "t value"]

# the reproduced specification under each rule: zero and drop from the curve,
# split and the two imputations from their comparison with the zero twin
ref_spec <- \(d) d |>
  dplyr::filter(outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "unemp", copredictor == "none",
         estimator == "fe_twoway", item_set == "all", cell_weight == "unweighted",
         measure == "wb_nat", pred_form == "raw")
spec <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  curve |> ref_spec() |> dplyr::transmute(rule = noop, b, r_ca, p = p_cr2, test = "CR2"),
  noop_rows |> ref_spec() |> datawizard::data_filter(noop == "zero", !on_curve) |>
    dplyr::transmute(rule = option, b = b_dev, r_ca = r_ca_dev, p = p_dev,
              test = dplyr::if_else(rule == "split", "CR2", "Rubin, clustered, 26 df"))
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rule = factor(rule, c("zero", "drop", "split", "mi_mice", "mi_amelia"))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("rule")
sp <- \(rl, col) spec[[col]][spec$rule == rl]

# the rules across the curve; each deviation off the curve is set beside both of
# its twins (zero and drop), so the specifications are counted once each
rule_specs <- noop_rows |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!on_curve) |>
  dplyr::distinct(option, outcome, copredictor, estimator, item_set, cell_weight, measure, pred_form) |>
  dplyr::count(option)
noop_lev <- noop_devs |>
  datawizard::data_filter(rule %in% c("cr2", "mi_rubin_cr1_g1")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(rule_specs, by = "option") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(specifications = dplyr::if_else(on_curve, n_pairs, n))

mi_spec <- mi |> datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "mcosmo", copredictor == "none", estimator == "fe_twoway",
                        sample == "all", reg_weight == "none")
n_mi_cells <- nrow(dplyr::distinct(mi, outcome, copredictor, estimator, sample, reg_weight))
clipped <- dg$value[dg$engine == "amelia_emb" & dg$quantity == "clipped draws share"]

# the sensitivity band: every silent respondent is assigned the answered mean of
# their cell plus delta; delta = 0 is the drop rule, and delta equal to minus the
# answered mean of each cell is the zero rule, which a common delta approximates
ans <- me |> datawizard::data_filter(construction == "share", item_set == "all", noop == "drop",
                    cell_weight == "unweighted", outcome == "mcosmo") |>
  dplyr::select(cntry, year, m_ans = value) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(pw |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("cntry", "year", "n_cy", "n_noop")), by = c("cntry", "year")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(cy |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("cntry", "year", "unemp")), by = c("cntry", "year")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(share_noop = n_noop / n_cy)
band <- purrr::map(seq(-0.6, 0.3, by = 0.05), \(d) {
  m <- fixest::feols(I(m_ans + share_noop * d) ~ unemp | cntry + year, data = ans, vcov = "iid")
  t <- fixest::coeftable(m)["unemp", "t value"]
  # the partial correlation by the conversion rule of the robustness study, r = t / sqrt(t^2 + df)
  tibble::tibble(delta = d, b = coef(m)[["unemp"]],
                 r = effectsize::t_to_r(t, fixest::degrees_freedom(m, type = "resid"))$r)
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
delta_zero <- -weighted.mean(ans$m_ans, ans$n_noop)
```

In the Europeanisation and the economy case study, every outcome on the [specification menu](../menu.qmd) is built from one survey question. The six scales offered by the full menu as its frame set are six ways of adding up the answers to that question, of which the curve of the claim retains the three positive ones. The menu treats the choice among the six scales as a decision about what the claim is about, and the choice of scoring rule – a share of a respondent's own mentions or a count of the items in the set – as a second decision of the same kind, without, however, presenting the instrument itself. This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) examines the thirteen answer options in turn. It considers how often each option is named, how the answers to the options relate to one another and how many dimensions the answers form. It then asks whether those dimensions are the four built by the original author of the case study and inherited by the course, how far a scale of two items can be trusted as a measure, and what becomes of the respondents who name none of the thirteen. Its subject is measurement rather than modelling, and nothing here changes which scales the course uses, for reasons given in section 8, but the module should leave you knowing more about the numbers before you choose one.

The tables of sections 1 to 9 are read from files written before the page was built. Since the respondent-level records are licensed by GESIS and are not distributed with the course, the analyses were run once, on the facilitator's machine, by `companion/_model-outputs/fit_measurement.R`, and only aggregate tables were committed: item prevalences, a correlation matrix, eigenvalues, loadings and fit indices. The correlation matrix suffices to repeat every exploratory step below without the microdata, as the [Try it](#try-it) at the end of the module does.

## 1. The instrument {#sec-instrument}

The question behind the scales is the Eurobarometer item asking "What does the European Union mean to you personally?", presented with a card of fourteen answers of which any number may be chosen, and it is the source of every framing scale in the case study. The original author sets one of the fourteen aside, the Euro, and builds the four scales from the remaining thirteen [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623], grounding the grouping in an earlier categorical principal component analysis of a single wave which had found that "these answer categories build four distinct dimensions of EU framing across the 27 EU countries" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. The construction of each scale is stated in one sentence: "For each of the framing dimensions, the scale is composed of the sum of the mentioned items belonging to the specific framing dimension, divided by the total number of items mentioned by the respondent", so that the four scales "measure the relative frequency with which the respondent associates each frame to the EU" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. That sentence corresponds to the share rule of the menu, while the count rule and the per-item rate are the two departures from it taken by the analysts of the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] and by the course.

@tbl-items lists the thirteen answers under the scale to which each was assigned, with the share of all `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` respondents who named it. To the four published scales the course adds two composites, a positive one combining the cosmopolitan and utilitarian items and a negative one combining the communitarian and libertarian items, because the claim under test speaks of positive and negative dimensions in the plural and singles out none of them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-items
#| tbl-cap: "The thirteen answer options, the scale each was assigned to in the original paper, and the share of respondents naming each. The 'Euro' option is the fourteenth and is set aside throughout, following the original paper. Shares are over all respondents interviewed in the sixteen waves, those who named nothing included."
prev |>
  datawizard::data_modify(scale = factor(scale, scale_order), valence = dplyr::if_else(valence == "positive", "positive", "negative")) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("scale") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Item = item, Scale = as.character(scale), Valence = valence, `Named by` = pct(share_mentioning)) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 4, align = "r")
```

Freedom to travel is the one answer given by about half of respondents, while the others are named by between roughly a tenth and three tenths, social protection and the loss of cultural identity being the rarest. These prevalences bear on what follows, because a scale is only as informative as the answers of which it is made, and a scale of two rarely named items has less to work with than a scale of five common ones.

## 2. The theory behind the grouping {#sec-theory}

The four published scales constitute a theory, stated before any correlation was computed, which the paper formulates in one sentence: the items "can be clustered into four distinct EU-framing dimensions endorsed by European citizens: two positive and two negative; two referring to a materialist and two related to a non-materialist understanding of the EU" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 620]. Two axes cross in this design, with valence separating the answers that praise the Union from those that blame it, and materialism separating the answers about money and welfare from those about peace, democracy, identity and borders. Each scale forms one cell of the resulting two-by-two, the utilitarian scale being "the positive materialist dimension", the libertarian scale "the negative materialist dimension", the cosmopolitan scale "the positive non-materialist dimension" and the communitarian scale "the negative non-materialist dimension" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 620].

The paper relies on that design again in its hypotheses, which is why the design is worth examining here. The first hypothesis comprises two sentences, of which only the first appears on the claim card of the robustness study: "Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 621]. The second sentence compares cells of the two-by-two with one another, a comparison presupposing that the two materialist scales and the two non-materialist scales are what the theory says they are. The second hypothesis, concerning the education gap, rests on the same presupposition in predicting that poor economic performance narrows the gap more on the materialist dimensions.

The sections that follow put to the data the question answered in advance by the theory, namely how the thirteen answers relate to one another and how many dimensions they form. The valence axis will be recovered clearly, the materialist axis only on one side of the valence line and not on the other, and section 8 considers what that leaves of the two sentences above. Neither kind of grouping is wrong in itself, a scale defined by theory being comparable with published work and with other analysts, which is what a replication needs, while a scale defined by the data fits the data from which it was cut. As the two groupings can disagree, and here partly do, the grouping on which a claim is tested is a decision made by the analyst, whether or not the decision is stated.

## 3. The correlations among the items {#sec-correlations}

Each answer is a yes or a no, and between two yes-or-no variables named by different shares of respondents the ordinary correlation cannot reach one. An item named by a quarter of respondents and an item named by half can thus never correlate at more than about 0.58 however closely the two items go together. The usual remedy in measurement work is the tetrachoric correlation, which treats each binary answer as the visible part of an underlying continuous propensity to give it and estimates the correlation between the two propensities. It is the correlation on which factor analysis of binary items is built, and @fig-tet presents all seventy-eight such correlations among the thirteen items, arranged with the two positive scales first and the two negative ones after.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tet
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| fig-cap: "Tetrachoric correlations among the thirteen items, times one hundred, over all respondents. Items are ordered by the scale they were assigned to: cosmopolitan and utilitarian above the line, communitarian and libertarian below it."
tet_plot <- tet |>
  datawizard::data_modify(item = factor(item, item_order), with = factor(with, rev(item_order)))
ggplot2::ggplot(tet_plot, ggplot2::aes(item, with, fill = tetrachoric)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = round(100 * tetrachoric)), size = 3,
            colour = dplyr::if_else(abs(tet_plot$tetrachoric) > 0.45, "white", "#1a1a1a")) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#96131b", mid = "white", high = "#0e3b6a", limits = c(-0.6, 0.6),
                       name = "tetrachoric r") +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 13 - 7 + 0.5, colour = "#3c4a56") +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 7.5, colour = "#3c4a56") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        legend.position = "right")
```

The items divide first by valence. The seven positive items correlate positively with one another, at between roughly `r num(min(tet$tetrachoric[tet$item %in% item_order[1:7] & tet$with %in% item_order[1:7] & tet$item != tet$with]))` and `r num(max(tet$tetrachoric[tet$item %in% item_order[1:7] & tet$with %in% item_order[1:7] & tet$item != tet$with]))`, the six negative items likewise at between `r num(min(tet$tetrachoric[tet$item %in% item_order[8:13] & tet$with %in% item_order[8:13] & tet$item != tet$with]))` and `r num(max(tet$tetrachoric[tet$item %in% item_order[8:13] & tet$with %in% item_order[8:13] & tet$item != tet$with]))`, and the correlations across the line are close to zero or mildly negative, the strongest of them being the `r num(tet_r("Economic prosperity", "Waste of money"))` between economic prosperity and waste of money. The original paper reports the same shape at the level of the four scales, with "the two positive EU framing and … the two negative EU-framing dimensions" associated at 0.27 and 0.26 and the associations across the valence line "low" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 625]. The item-level matrix also shows where the structure within each valence lies. On the negative side the two libertarian items, bureaucracy and waste of money, correlate at `r num(tet_r("Bureaucracy", "Waste of money"))` with each other and more weakly with the communitarian four, while more crime and border control correlate at `r num(tet_r("More crime", "Not enough border control"))`. On the positive side the strongest pairs, social protection with economic prosperity at `r num(tet_r("Social protection", "Economic prosperity"))`, peace with democracy at `r num(tet_r("Peace", "Democracy"))` and freedom to travel with cultural diversity at `r num(tet_r("Freedom to travel", "Cultural diversity"))`, each lie within a published scale, but democracy correlates with social protection at `r num(tet_r("Democracy", "Social protection"))` and with freedom to travel at only `r num(tet_r("Democracy", "Freedom to travel"))`, so that the utilitarian pair are more closely related to peace and democracy than are freedom to travel and cultural diversity, the two mobility items of the cosmopolitan scale to which peace and democracy also belong. This pattern is the first indication of a structure made explicit by the factor analysis below.

The unemployment item, counted by the original paper among the communitarian meanings of the EU, bears on a decision elsewhere on the menu. It correlates at `r num(tet_r("Unemployment", "Economic prosperity"))` with economic prosperity and at `r num(tet_r("Unemployment", "Freedom to travel"))` with freedom to travel. It is also the item removed from the communitarian scale by a robustness check in the paper, because "it could be theoretically argued that unemployment does not constitute a component of a communitarian understanding of the EU" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 633, fn. 5], a removal that the menu offers as its item-set decision.

## 4. Dimensions {#sec-dimensions}

A correlation matrix of thirteen items has thirteen eigenvalues, whose sizes indicate how much of the shared variation among the items a given number of underlying dimensions would account for. As @fig-eigen shows, the first two eigenvalues stand well clear of the rest, at `r num(eig$eigenvalue[1])` and `r num(eig$eigenvalue[2])`, a third lies at `r num(eig$eigenvalue[3])`, and every later eigenvalue falls below one, the conventional threshold for a dimension worth retaining.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eigen
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Eigenvalues of the tetrachoric matrix (points), with the mean eigenvalue of random data of the same size (dashed) from a parallel analysis. With over four hundred thousand respondents the random benchmark is almost exactly one, so the parallel analysis is a formality here, and what matters is the size of the gaps between the eigenvalues."
ggplot2::ggplot(eig, ggplot2::aes(factor, eigenvalue)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = parallel_mean), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5b6b78") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2.2) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "#b7c2cc") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:13) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "dimension", y = "eigenvalue") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Read as a count of dimensions, the figure suggests two with a possible third, a count resting on the items alone, without any assumption about which answers belong together. Two dimensions would correspond to the valence split already shown by the correlation matrix, and the next section asks whether a third and a fourth correspond to the published split within each valence. The parallel analysis usually consulted at this point, which compares each eigenvalue with what random data of the same dimensions would produce, suggests five, but with `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` respondents the random benchmark is almost exactly one for every dimension, and the criterion thus reduces to counting eigenvalues above one, adding little at this sample size.

## 5. Exploratory solutions {#sec-efa}

Exploratory factor analysis asks which underlying dimensions, unconstrained by any prior assignment, best reproduce the correlations among the items, and reports for each item how strongly it belongs to each dimension. The solutions below were extracted by minimum-residual factoring from the tetrachoric matrix and rotated obliquely, which allows the dimensions to correlate with one another as substantive dimensions of an attitude generally do. @tbl-efa4 presents the four-factor solution, with the assignment made in the original paper beside each item and loadings below 0.30 left blank so that the structure can be read at a glance, while the two-factor solution is described in the prose that follows it.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-efa4
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_efa4
show <- function(x) dplyr::if_else(abs(x) < 0.30, "", num(x))
l4 |>
  datawizard::data_modify(item = factor(item, item_order)) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("item") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Item = as.character(item), `Published scale` = scale,
            `Factor 1` = show(F1), `Factor 2` = show(F2), `Factor 3` = show(F3), `Factor 4` = show(F4),
            Communality = num(communality)) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:7, align = "r")
```

Two of the four factors reproduce the two negative scales of the original paper, item for item. The communitarian four – unemployment, loss of cultural identity, more crime and border control – load on one factor and on nothing else, with more crime the strongest at `r num(ld("More crime", "F2"))`, while bureaucracy and waste of money load on a factor of their own at `r num(ld("Bureaucracy", "F3"))` and `r num(ld("Waste of money", "F3"))`. The two negative factors are distinct and related, correlating at `r num(phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F2"])`, which is the pattern one would want from two dimensions of a single negative stance towards the EU. On the positive side, however, the published split is not reproduced. Peace, democracy, economic prosperity and social protection form one factor, cutting across the line between cosmopolitan and utilitarian framing, with the two utilitarian items loading highest on it, and freedom to travel and cultural diversity form another, with stronger say in the world divided between the two positive factors at `r num(ld("Stronger say in the world", "F1"))` and `r num(ld("Stronger say in the world", "F4"))`. Read substantively, the data appear to split the positive meanings of the EU not into a civic and an economic set but into a set of benefits that the EU delivers, peace and democracy alongside prosperity and protection, and a set of things that the EU lets one do and be, travel and diversity, with a stronger say in the world belonging a little to each. The two positive factors correlate at `r num(phi4$F4[phi4$factor == "F1"])`, a value lower than the correlation between the two negative ones.

The two-factor solution, simpler still, is the solution to which the eigenvalues point first. Every positive item loads on one factor, at between `r num(min(l2$F2[l2$valence == "positive"]))` and `r num(max(l2$F2[l2$valence == "positive"]))`, every negative item on the other, at between `r num(min(l2$F1[l2$valence == "negative"]))` and `r num(max(l2$F1[l2$valence == "negative"]))`, no item loads above 0.30 on the wrong side, and the two factors correlate at `r num(phi2$F2[phi2$factor == "F1"])`. The result is a clean valence structure, which underlies the two composites added by the course. A positive scale of seven items and a negative scale of six are what the instrument most plainly measures, and each of the finer scales is a subset of one of these two.

## 6. A confirmatory comparison {#sec-cfa}

Since an exploratory solution is chosen by the data, it is bound to fit the data from which it was chosen. A confirmatory model, by contrast, states an assignment of items to dimensions in advance and asks how far the correlations implied by that assignment depart from the correlations found. @tbl-cfa compares three such models, fitted to the binary items by diagonally weighted least squares, the estimator built for this kind of data: the published four-scale model, the four-factor model read off @tbl-efa4 with stronger say in the world allowed to belong to both positive factors, and the two-factor valence model. The indices are the usual ones, the comparative fit index and the Tucker–Lewis index reading upward towards one, and the root mean square error of approximation and the standardised root mean square residual reading downward towards zero. By the customary thresholds a comparative fit index above 0.95 and a root mean square error below 0.05 count as good, while the chi-square is reported for completeness only, because with `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` respondents it rejects every model that is not exactly true.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cfa
#| tbl-cap: "Three confirmatory models of the thirteen items, fitted on all respondents with the diagonally weighted least squares estimator and robust corrections. The data-driven model is the four-factor exploratory structure refitted as a confirmatory one, and is expected to fit better than the published model on the data it was read from."
cfa |>
  datawizard::data_modify(model = c(published = "Published four scales", data_driven = "Data-driven four factors", valence = "Two valence factors")[model]) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Model = model, `Chi-square (df)` = sprintf("%s (%d)", format(round(chisq), big.mark = ","), as.integer(df)),
            CFI = num(cfi, 3), TLI = num(tli, 3), RMSEA = num(rmsea, 3), SRMR = num(srmr, 3)) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:6, align = "r")
```

The three models fall in the order that the exploratory analysis leads one to expect, none of them reaching the conventional threshold of 0.95 on the comparative fit index. The data-driven model performs best on every index, with a comparative fit index of `r num(fit("data_driven", "cfi"), 3)` against `r num(fit("published", "cfi"), 3)` for the published scales and `r num(fit("valence", "cfi"), 3)` for the valence model, and the root mean square error is below 0.05 for all three, at `r num(fit("data_driven", "rmsea"), 3)`, `r num(fit("published", "rmsea"), 3)` and `r num(fit("valence", "rmsea"), 3)`. On this evidence the published scales appear to be a defensible reading of the items, though not a privileged one. A structure read off the data fits better, as it is bound to, the difference between the two structures being confined to the positive side, where economic prosperity and social protection load with peace and democracy instead of forming a scale of their own. At the same time, the finer structure improves on the valence split by a margin that is real but modest, and a reader who prefers the two composites for their reliability, quantified in the next section, or for their fit to the wording of the claim, thus gives up less than the four-scale vocabulary suggests.

## 7. Reliability {#sec-reliability}

How far a short scale, such as one of two answers, can be trusted as a measure of a single disposition is a standard question in measurement, to which a reliability coefficient provides the answer. For the four published scales and the two composites, @tbl-rel reports the number of items, their mean tetrachoric correlation and the ordinal alpha that follows from the two, namely Cronbach's alpha computed on the tetrachoric rather than the ordinary correlations and read on the same scale, on which one corresponds to perfect consistency among the items.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rel
#| tbl-cap: "Reliability of the six scales on the menu, from the tetrachoric correlations among their items. Ordinal alpha is Cronbach's alpha computed on the tetrachoric matrix. Mean prevalence is the average share of respondents naming an item of the scale."
rel |>
  datawizard::data_modify(scale = factor(scale, c(scale_order, "positive", "negative"))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("scale") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Scale = as.character(scale), Items = items, `Mean tetrachoric r` = num(mean_tetrachoric),
            `Ordinal alpha` = num(ordinal_alpha), `Mean prevalence` = pct(mean_prevalence)) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

The two composites are the most reliable constructs on the menu, at `r num(alpha("positive"))` and `r num(alpha("negative"))`, because reliability grows with the number of items as well as with their agreement. The two two-item scales are the least reliable, the utilitarian at `r num(alpha("utilitarian"))` and the libertarian at `r num(alpha("libertarian"))`, although the two libertarian items agree with each other more closely than do the items of either positive scale. In the country-year panel on which the course fits its models, a low reliability means that the cell mean of a two-item scale is noisier for the same number of respondents, making an association with unemployment harder to detect on the utilitarian scale than on the cosmopolitan one, for a reason unrelated to whether the association exists. Reliability is a property of the construct, which is why the menu does not offer it as a choice, but it still bears on the choice of outcome and is one of the reasons for the care with which the outcome axis is read on the results page.

## 8. Consequences for the menu {#sec-menu}

When the results are set against the theory of section 2, the valence axis is recovered in full, the first division among the items being between praise and blame. The materialist axis is recovered on the negative side, where the communitarian and libertarian items come apart exactly as the paper assigns them, and not on the positive side, where the items divide into the benefits that the Union delivers (peace, democracy, prosperity, social protection) and the mobility and diversity that it permits (freedom to travel, cultural diversity), a line that cuts across the utilitarian and cosmopolitan scales. The second sentence of the first hypothesis, "the effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions", is thereby left as a comparison in which one of the two materialist scales is supported by the data and the other is a theoretical grouping not reproduced by the data. As the claim card received by the analysts of the robustness study contained the first sentence only, none of the five reanalyses tested the comparison. Nor is the comparison tested by the course, whose [background page](../background.qmd#sec-questions) presents the sentence of the paper from which the claim was taken, while the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd) and the exercise page of each format explain why choosing which sentence to replicate is itself the first specification decision.

The full menu retains the four published scales and the two composites as its frame set, in the knowledge of what the analyses on this page show about each of the six scales. The published scales are the vocabulary of the claim under test and of the five reanalyses, and comparability with both is worth more to a replication exercise than a structure that fits a little better on the data from which it was read. The two negative scales are, in any case, recovered by the data item for item. The composites, added by the course, arguably have the strongest support in the items: the valence split is the first thing the eigenvalues show, the two-factor solution is clean, and the composites are the most reliable scales on the menu. The curve of the claim retains three of the six scales, the cosmopolitan and utilitarian scales and the positive composite, because the claim names the positive dimensions, and section 9 explains what became of the three negative scales. This page argues against treating the assignment of items to scales as a further fork of the multiverse. Which items make up 'cosmopolitan framing' is a question about the validity of a measure of a named construct, and the evidence above is the right kind of evidence for that question. As the question of which construct the claim is about is a separate matter, a menu offering alternative groupings as options would be asking participants to settle by choice a question already addressed by the item analyses.

The scoring rule is a different kind of decision, one about the question itself, since whether a respondent's answers enter as a share of their own mentions or as a count of the items in the set changes what 'more cosmopolitan framing' means, and no analysis of the items can settle it. The [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimand) presents the three rules as a decision about the question, and section 9 gives the reasons why the count and the rate left the curve.

## 9. The outcome on the curve {#sec-curve-outcome}

When the course asked of every option on its menu whether it is a justifiable way of answering the claim, read as a claim about change within countries over time, three of the decisions made on this page came out in a way not shown by the full menu. The [decision map](../menu.qmd#map) presents every option of every decision, on the curve and off it, and the [specification menu](../menu.qmd) provides the reasoning for each, while this section examines the three that concern the construction of the outcome. The numbers are drawn from the curve of the claim (`data/spec_curve.csv`), the curve of the negative scales (`data/spec_curve_negative.csv`) and the comparison of every option of the full menu with its twins on the curve (`data/menu_deviations.csv`), all fitted on country-year aggregates and classed, like every point of the curve, by CR2 errors clustered by country with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

### The negative scales {#sec-negative}

The claim under test names the positive dimensions of framing, and the hypothesis from which it was taken has a second half, that poor economic performance increases the negative ones [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 621]. The communitarian and libertarian scales and the negative composite address that second half on a curve of their own, comprising the same `r nrow(neg)` specifications and drawn on the [Specification curve page](../curve.qmd#negative-scales) beside the curve of the claim. On the negative curve, `r pp(below_sig(neg))` of the specifications lie in the direction of the hypothesis with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pp(below_sig(curve))` on the curve of the claim. The two curves are not independent confirmations, for the reasons given under [Frame set](../menu.qmd#frame-set) in the specification menu and in the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-europeanisation). Reversed so that it points the way of the claim, the negative composite is the positive composite plus the rate of saying nothing, and once the mean of each country is removed the two correlate at `r num(cor(cell_wide$pos_within, cell_wide$neg_within))` across the 270 country-years. The communitarian scale contains the item 'unemployment', which ties the outcome to the predictor by content, and at the reproduced specification its claim-aligned partial correlation is `r num(r_at(neg, "mcomm"), 3)` with all thirteen items and `r num(r_at(neg, "mcomm", "un"), 3)` without that one. The libertarian scale moves little with the economy, `r pp(below_sig(dplyr::filter(neg, outcome == "mlib")))` of its specifications lying in the direction of the hypothesis with CR2 p < 0.05 against `r pp(below_sig(dplyr::filter(neg, outcome == "mcomm")))` of the communitarian ones.

### Count and rate {#sec-count}

The paper scores each scale as a share of the respondent's mentions, and the curve retains that rule because the claim concerns how citizens frame the EU, a matter of composition, as the section [Scoring rule](../menu.qmd#scoring-rule) of the specification menu explains. A count of the scale items mentioned by a respondent measures how much the respondent says about the EU in that register, and across the 270 country-years it mostly tracks how much respondents say about the EU at all. The cosmopolitan count correlates at `r num(cor(cell_wide$count_mcosmo, cell_wide$total))` with the mean number of items mentioned by respondents in the cell, the cosmopolitan share at `r num(cor(cell_wide$share_mcosmo, cell_wide$total))`, and the two versions of the same scale with each other at only `r num(cor(cell_wide$share_mcosmo, cell_wide$count_mcosmo))`. The count is the construct used by the reanalysts KEVF1 and 018OL, and the per-item rate, the count divided by the number of items in the scale, answers the same question about volume, since dividing by a constant leaves the test and the partial correlation of a linear model unchanged. Swapped into the `r dv("count", "n_pairs")` specifications of the curve, the count leaves `r pp(dv("count", "below_zero"))` of them below zero but only `r pp(dv("count", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pp(below_sig(curve))` on the curve itself, and it changes the class of `r pp(dv("count", "class_changes"))` of the pairs. At the reproduced specification the claim-aligned partial correlation falls from `r num(r_at(curve, "mcosmo"), 3)` with the share to `r num(count_ref$r_ca_dev, 3)` with the count, with a CR2 p-value of `r num(count_ref$p_dev, 2)`.

### The item set {#sec-item-set}

Both item sets remain on the curve, for reasons given in the section [Item set](../menu.qmd#item-set) of the specification menu. The thirteen items are the published measure, and the set without 'unemployment' removes a content overlap between outcome and predictor, since the item enters the denominator of every share and a rise in its mentions mechanically lowers every other share. The original paper removes the item from the communitarian scale in a robustness check [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 633, fn. 5], while the set used by the course drops it from every denominator. On the curve of the claim, `r pp(below_sig(dplyr::filter(curve, item_set == "all")))` of the specifications with all thirteen items lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pp(below_sig(dplyr::filter(curve, item_set == "un")))` of those without the item. The decision carries `r pp(fk("item_set"))` of the variance of the curve, moving it alone changes the class of `r pp(fk("item_set", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs of specifications that differ in nothing else, and at the reproduced specification the claim-aligned partial correlation moves from `r num(r_at(curve, "mcosmo"), 3)` to `r num(r_at(curve, "mcosmo", "un"), 3)`. The difference between the two sets corresponds to the part of the result carried by the overlap, and the curve retains both sets so that the size of that part remains visible.

## 10. Respondents who mention nothing {#sec-noop}

The [specification menu](../menu.qmd) includes a decision called **respondents who mention nothing**, with five options, whose presence this section and the next explain. Of the `r format(n_all, big.mark = ",")` respondents, `r format(n_noop, big.mark = ",")` (`r pp(100 * n_noop / n_all)`) answered the question of section 1 by mentioning none of the thirteen items, their score on every framing scale thus being zero divided by zero. The original paper and its five reanalyses resolved this difficulty in two different ways, mostly without saying so, and the people concerned are not a random slice of the sample. The curve of the claim retains both common rules, scoring the silent respondents zero and leaving them out, while the other three options are taught here beside those two rules.

The survey records two further codes for a respondent who ticks nothing, "other (spontaneous)" and "don't know", and the `r format(n_noop, big.mark = ",")` silent respondents split three ways. Of these respondents, `r format(n_dk, big.mark = ",")` said that they did not know, `r format(n_oth, big.mark = ",")` gave an answer that was not on the list, and `r format(n_bl, big.mark = ",")` have no tick of any kind. These are three different kinds of respondent. Someone who says that the EU means something not anticipated by the list has an opinion, while someone who says that they do not know may have none, or may have one that they would rather not state. A blank row may be a refusal, an omission by the interviewer or a coding gap, and the file does not say which.

The Stata code written by the original author divides the number of mentions in each framing cluster by the total number of mentions and has no rule for a zero total. As Stata returns a missing value for 0/0 and the mixed model drops a missing outcome, those respondents left the original analysis without a line of code saying so. The level-1 N of 390,373 reported by the original author, the number of respondents in the model, is exactly the number who mentioned at least one item. The code of the reanalyst KQXUE drops the silent respondents in the same way. The reanalysis that produced the t of −3.804 recorded in the robustness study coded the same respondents 0 on every scale, a convention inherited by the course panel, while KEVF1 and 018OL, who built a count and a mean of the cosmopolitan items rather than a share, score them 0 by construction. PRL47 built both versions and reported model B8, which uses the version without those respondents. The published coefficient and its best-known reanalysis thus differ in what they assume about `r pp(100 * n_noop / n_all)` of the sample, and neither states the assumption.

Whether the difference matters depends on who the silent respondents are and on which comparison the analysis makes. The silent respondents are older and more often women, and across the `r nrow(pw)` cells the no-opinion rate correlates at `r num(r_noop_unemp, 2)` with the unemployment rate and at `r num(r_noop_cosmo, 2)` with the cosmopolitan scale. The rate also differs sharply between countries, standing at `r pp(100 * by_c$rate[1])` in `r by_c$cntry[1]` and `r pp(100 * by_c$rate[2])` in `r by_c$cntry[2]` against `r pp(100 * by_c$rate[nrow(by_c)])` in `r by_c$cntry[nrow(by_c)]`. Those correlations are dominated by stable differences between countries, removed by the fixed-effects designs of the curve. Within countries, net of the movement common to all of them in a year, the rate falls slightly as unemployment rises (`r num(noop_b, 4)` per point of unemployment, t = `r num(noop_t, 1)` with conventional errors and `r num(noop_t_cl, 2)` with errors clustered by country), and scoring the silent as zero thus pulls the slopes of the curve a little towards zero rather than in the direction of the claim.

@tbl-noop-countries lists the four highest and the four lowest rates, each averaged over the years of its country.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-noop-countries
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The four highest and four lowest no-opinion rates, each averaged over the years of its country. Source: `data/teney_panel_weights.csv`."
tinytable::tt(
  by_c |> dplyr::slice(c(1:4, (dplyr::n() - 3):dplyr::n())) |>
    dplyr::transmute(Country = cntry, `No opinion` = pp(100 * rate))) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

### The three rules {#sec-noop-rules}

The menu offers three deterministic rules, which code every silent respondent in the same way without fitting a model, each amounting to a statement about what the silent respondents mean. **Zero** treats them as people with no framing of any kind, the convention of the course panel and of the reproduced specification. **Drop** treats them as people who did not answer the question, as the code of the original author did. **Split** takes the three codes at their word: "don't know" and blank are dropped as non-response, and "other" is kept at zero, on the reasoning that an answer off the list is still an answer that contains no cosmopolitan content. The rules change the cell means before any model is fitted, the average cosmopolitan cell mean being `r num(mean(me$value[me$construction == "share" & me$item_set == "all" & me$noop == "zero" & me$cell_weight == "unweighted" & me$outcome == "mcosmo"]), 3)` under zero and `r num(mean(me$value[me$construction == "share" & me$item_set == "all" & me$noop == "drop" & me$cell_weight == "unweighted" & me$outcome == "mcosmo"]), 3)` under drop.

The rules also change the question. Under zero the estimand is the average framing among everyone interviewed, with silence counted as no framing, and the cell mean then equals the share among those who answered multiplied by the proportion who answered, so that the rate of saying nothing enters every scale. Under drop the estimand is the average framing among people who have a framing at all, which suits the share as a measure, since a respondent with no mentions has no share, at the cost of conditioning on answering. As these are different populations, the no-opinion rule is an estimand decision by the test applied in the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#what-each-decision-commits-you-to). The rule is classed with measurement on the menu because that is where the decision is made in practice, at the moment the outcome column is built, and a participant who meets the decision there should know that it also changes the estimand. Both rules remain on the curve, zero because the reproduction task rests on it and drop because it matches the construct and the code of the original study. Split is kept off the curve, since its construct is no clearer than that of either rule and its results lie close to those of the two rules.

Across the curve, the rule moves the share of specifications that lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 by a few points and the median correlation by a few hundredths:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-noop-levels
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The no-opinion rules across the curve of the claim. Zero and drop are the two halves of the curve; split and the two imputations are swapped into the specifications to which they apply, the imputations only at the standard measurement settings. Sources: `data/menu_deviations.csv` and `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz`."
tinytable::tt(
  noop_lev |>
    datawizard::data_modify(option = factor(option, c("zero", "drop", "split", "mi_mice", "mi_amelia"),
                           labels = c("zero", "drop", "split", "imputed (mice)", "imputed (Amelia)"))) |>
    datawizard::data_arrange("option") |>
    dplyr::transmute(`No-opinion rule` = option,
              `On the curve` = dplyr::if_else(on_curve, "yes", "no"),
              Specifications = format(specifications, big.mark = ","),
              `Below zero` = pp(below_zero),
              `Below zero, p < 0.05` = pp(below_zero_sig),
              `Median aligned r` = num(median_r_ca, 3),
              Test = dplyr::if_else(rule == "cr2", "CR2", "Rubin, clustered, 26 df"))) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:6, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

For the reproduced specification, the coefficient on unemployment for cosmopolitan framing, with two-way fixed effects on all 270 cells, takes the following values under the five rules:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-noop-spec
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The reproduced C6HJR specification under each treatment of the respondents who mentioned nothing. Zero is the reproduced result; the imputed variants are tested by their clustered t pooled over ten imputations, since the imputation tier holds no CR2 test. Sources: `data/spec_curve.csv` and `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz`."
tinytable::tt(
  spec |>
    dplyr::transmute(Rule = c(zero = "zero (robustness study, course panel)", drop = "drop (original paper)",
                       split = "split", mi_mice = "imputed, mice",
                       mi_amelia = "imputed, Amelia")[as.character(rule)],
              b = num(b, 5), `aligned r` = num(r_ca, 3), p = num(p, 3), Test = test)) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

Under zero the reproduced result has a CR2 p-value of `r num(sp("zero", "p"), 3)`, and under drop the same specification yields a stronger association, r = `r num(sp("drop", "r_ca"), 3)` against `r num(sp("zero", "r_ca"), 3)`, with p = `r num(sp("drop", "p"), 3)`. Across the curve the drop half has `r pp(below_sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, noop == "drop")))` of its specifications below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 and the zero half `r pp(below_sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, noop == "zero")))`, a difference corresponding to the pull towards zero predicted by the within-country fall of the no-opinion rate.

## 11. Multiple imputation {#sec-imputation}

Imputation replaces a rule with a model. Instead of deciding what the silent would have said, it estimates a distribution for each missing score from the observed characteristics of the respondent and draws from it, several times over, so that the uncertainty of the guess is included in the final standard error. @Dong2013Principled describe the three steps: fill the gaps m times to produce m complete datasets, analyse each with the model you would have run anyway, and combine the m results with the rules given by @Rubin1987Imputation, under which the pooled estimate is the mean of the m estimates and its variance is the mean within-imputation variance plus the between-imputation variance inflated by a factor of 1 + 1/m. The between-imputation part expresses the uncertainty about the imputed values, and a single imputation, which sets that part to zero, understates every standard error computed from the imputed data. How many imputations are enough depends on how much information is missing. @Graham2007Many show that the once-standard three to five are too few when the fraction of missing information is not small, and the course uses ten. The imputation model should include every variable in the analysis model and anything else that predicts either the missing values or their missingness [@CollinsEtAl2001ComparisonInclusiveRestrictive; @Schafer2002View], and it should not be *less* general than the analysis model, a condition named 'congeniality' by @Meng1994Imputation and one that is easy to violate here, since the imputation happens at respondent level and the analysis at cell level.

Whether such a model can stand in for the missing answers depends on why the answers are missing, and the vocabulary for describing the reasons comes from @Rubin1976InferenceMissingData, presented accessibly by @Dong2013Principled. Data are **missing completely at random** when the probability that a value is missing depends on nothing in the data at all, in which case the observed cases are a random sample of the complete ones and dropping the incomplete cases costs precision and nothing else. Data are **missing at random** when that probability depends on things that were observed but not, once those are accounted for, on the missing value itself. Data are **missing not at random** when the probability depends on the missing value even after the observed data are allowed for. The labels describe the mechanism that produced the gaps rather than their size, and their practical consequence is asymmetric, in that the first two can be handled with methods using only the observed data, whereas the third requires the analyst to state how the missing values differ from the observed ones, which the data cannot reveal.

Mapped onto the case study, the silent respondents are plainly not missing completely at random, since their age, sex and location predict their silence. Missing at random given age, sex, education and the country-year cell is the working assumption on which every imputation below rests. The assumption is not testable from the observed data alone, a point made by @Dong2013Principled against the habit of reading a t-test on observed covariates as a test of it. What can be done is to make the assumption more plausible by conditioning on everything that predicts silence, and then to ask how far the conclusion moves if the assumption is wrong, the last step corresponding to the sensitivity band at the end of this section. A "don't know" about what the EU means is a fair candidate for missing not at random, because the people least engaged with the EU are the people least likely to have a framing of it, and disengagement is not in the data.

Two imputation engines are run on the case study, because they come from different traditions and the course should present both. **mice** [@Buuren2011Mice] imputes one variable at a time conditional on the others, cycling until the imputations settle, and the version used here draws each missing share from respondents with similar predicted values (predictive mean matching), which keeps every imputed score inside the range that a bounded scale can take [@White2010Imputation]. **Amelia** [@HonakerEtAl2011AmeliaIIProgram; @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical] fits one multivariate normal model to all the variables at once by expectation maximisation (an iterative algorithm for fitting a model to incomplete data) with bootstrapping, the approach developed by Gary King and colleagues for time-series cross-section data of this shape [@HonakerKing2010WhatMissingValues]. Amelia imputes by drawing from that model, and the imputed values can fall outside the unit interval and are then clipped, as `r pp(100 * clipped)` of its draws were here. Both engines condition on age, sex, education and the country and year of interview. Each of the ten completed respondent files is aggregated to country-year means, and the models are fitted on each and pooled at the standard measurement settings, for `r format(n_mi_cells, big.mark = ",")` combinations of outcome, adjustment, estimator, sample and regression weight, among them designs and samples not retained on the curve. Because the imputations exist only at those settings, they cannot be crossed with the rest of the menu and remain off the curve, serving as a check on the two rules that the curve retains.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mi
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The reproduced specification under multiple imputation, pooled over ten imputations by Rubin's rules, with conventional and with clustered errors. The fraction of missing information is the share of the uncertainty about the coefficient that is due to the silent respondents. Source: `data/spec_grid_mi.csv`."
tinytable::tt(
  mi_spec |>
    datawizard::data_select(select = c("engine", "se", "estimate", "statistic", "fmi")) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = se, values_from = c(estimate, statistic, fmi)) |>
    dplyr::transmute(Engine = c(mice_pmm = "mice, predictive mean matching",
                         amelia_emb = "Amelia, EM with bootstrapping")[engine],
              b = num(estimate_conventional, 5),
              `t, conventional` = num(statistic_conventional, 2),
              `t, clustered` = num(statistic_clustered, 2),
              `Fraction of missing information` = num(fmi_conventional, 3))) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

The two engines yield estimates close to one another and close to the drop rule, which is what should happen when the imputation model conditions on the same characteristics that distinguish the silent from the rest. Under missing at random, filling the gaps from people who resemble the silent respondents is a more careful version of leaving them out. The gap between the imputed rows and the zero row of @tbl-noop-spec corresponds to the part of the reproduced result removed by the zero convention.

### "Don't know" as an answer {#sec-dont-know}

Survey methodologists have argued for fifty years about whether a "don't know" is missing data or a response. @Francis1975Know reviewed the early evidence; @Krosnick2001Impact showed experimentally that offering an explicit no-opinion option does not, in general, improve the quality of the answers that remain, because many who take it could have answered; and @Luskin2011Know found the reverse for factual knowledge, where "don't know" mostly does mean not knowing. @Kuha2018Effect distinguish three ways of asking (encouraging a "don't know", accepting one neutrally, and probing it with a follow-up) and show on European Social Survey data that probing halves the rate but changes the measurement properties of the answers it extracts, so that the survey has traded an error of omission for an error of commission. The ESS itself does not probe. Who says "don't know" is not random either, and @Laurison2015WillingnessStateOpinion finds the willingness to state an opinion patterned by class and education, a pattern that makes non-response on attitude items a form of inequality in whose views reach the data.

That literature has two implications for this case study. It supports treating a "don't know" about the EU as non-response rather than as zero framing, which is what the drop rule, the split rule and the imputations do. It also warns that a group defined by not answering cannot be assumed to resemble the group that did, so the missing-at-random assumption behind imputation is where a critic would press. The "other" code in the battery is more reassuring, since `r format(n_oth, big.mark = ",")` people volunteered a meaning not offered by the list, and each of those answers is an opinion.

### Sensitivity to the assumption {#sec-sensitivity}

Nothing in the observed data can distinguish missing at random from missing not at random, and @Molenberghs2008Missingness prove that for any model of data missing not at random there is a model of data missing at random that fits the observed data equally well. The response is to show how far the conclusion depends on the assumption, and the device used here is a sensitivity band. Suppose every silent respondent would have scored what the answering respondents in their cell scored, plus some amount δ that is the same for all of them. Then each cell mean is the answered mean plus δ times the share of the cell that was silent, and the reproduced specification can be refitted for any δ. Two values are already familiar. δ = 0 is the drop rule, and the zero rule sets δ to minus the answered mean of each cell, a quantity averaging about `r num(delta_zero, 2)`, and a common δ of that size thus approximates the zero rule.

```{r}
#| label: fig-delta
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "The partial correlation of cosmopolitan framing with unemployment, two-way fixed effects, when every silent respondent is assigned the answered mean of their cell plus δ. Zero on the horizontal axis is the drop rule; the dashed line marks the average δ of the zero rule, and the burgundy point the zero rule itself, which applies a different δ to each cell. Sources: `data/teney_panel_measurement.csv`, `data/teney_panel_weights.csv` and `data/spec_curve.csv`."
minus <- function(x) gsub("-", "−", format(x), fixed = TRUE)
ggplot2::ggplot(band, ggplot2::aes(delta, r)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#848c94", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = delta_zero, colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = 2) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::annotate("point", x = delta_zero, y = sp("zero", "r_ca"), colour = "#8b1538", size = 2.4) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 0.02, y = max(band$r), hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "#848c94",
           label = "δ = 0: drop rule") +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = delta_zero + 0.02, y = sp("zero", "r_ca"), hjust = 0, size = 3.1,
           colour = "#8b1538", label = "zero rule, cell by cell") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = minus) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = minus) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "δ: assumed shortfall of the silent respondents, in scale units",
       y = "partial r") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The band changes in one direction only. The further the silent respondents are assumed to fall short of those who answered, the weaker the association, from r = `r num(band$r[which.max(band$delta)], 3)` at δ = `r num(max(band$delta), 1)` through `r num(band$r[which.min(abs(band$delta))], 3)` at δ = 0 to `r num(band$r[which.min(band$delta)], 3)` at δ = `r num(min(band$delta), 1)`. The zero convention, which assumes that everyone who stayed silent would have scored the lowest value allowed by the scale, is the most extreme assumption permitted by the bounds of the scale, and among the assumptions permitted by those bounds it moves the result furthest towards zero. As every value on the band remains below zero, the direction of the association does not depend on the assumption, whereas its strength does, and that dependence is what should be reported alongside a result on these data. Reporting the missing-data treatment, the assumption it makes and the sensitivity of the result to that assumption is what @Lee2021Framework and @Sterne2009Imputation ask for in observational research, and the proportion of missing data is not, on its own, the thing to report [@MadleyDowd2019Proportion].

## Try it {#try-it}

The committed correlation matrix is all that the exploratory analyses need. The code below rebuilds it from `companion/_model-outputs/items_tetrachoric.csv`, refits the four-factor solution of @tbl-efa4, and then asks for three factors, which is the solution that the eigenvalues leave open and which the page does not show. Where stronger say in the world goes, and which of the two positive factors survives when only one is allowed beside the two negative ones, is the question to answer.

```r
R <- readr::read_csv("companion/_model-outputs/items_tetrachoric.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = with, values_from = tetrachoric) |>
  tibble::column_to_rownames("item") |>
  as.matrix()
n <- 416698

psych::fa(R, nfactors = 4, n.obs = n, fm = "minres", rotate = "oblimin")   # the table above
psych::fa(R, nfactors = 3, n.obs = n, fm = "minres", rotate = "oblimin")   # the open question
```

A second exercise stays closer to the menu. Fit the four-factor solution with a varimax rotation instead, which forces the factors to be uncorrelated, and compare the loadings of the two negative factors with the oblique ones above. The difference reflects the correlation of `r num(phi4$F3[phi4$factor == "F2"])` between them.

Three exercises on the respondents who mention nothing use the files of sections 10 and 11.

1. From `teney_panel_weights.csv`, plot the no-opinion rate against the unemployment rate across the 270 cells and describe the pattern in one sentence. Which mechanism does it rule out? Then remove the country means from both variables and plot again. What changes, and why does the second plot matter more for the curve of the claim?
2. Find your preregistered specification in `data/spec_curve.csv` and its twin under the other rule, which differs only in `noop`. Then look up its split twin in `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz` (`axis == "noop"`, `option == "split"`). Which rule is the split rule closest to, and why would you expect that from what it does with the three kinds of silent respondent?
3. Rewrite the estimand statement for the zero rule and for the drop rule. Which word changes?

## Sources and provenance {#sec-sources}

The question wording, the assignment of items to the four scales and the share rule are taken from the original paper behind the Europeanisation case study [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, pp. 623 and 625], and the removal of the unemployment item as a robustness check from the fifth footnote of that paper. Every number in sections 1 to 8 was computed by `companion/_model-outputs/fit_measurement.R` on the respondent-level rebuild of the sixteen GESIS waves described in the [module on panel data](panel-data.qmd#sec-sources), with the tetrachoric correlations and the exploratory solutions from the psych package and the confirmatory models from lavaan, and only the aggregate tables written by the script are committed: the prevalences, the tetrachoric matrix, the eigenvalues with their parallel-analysis benchmark, the loadings and factor correlations of the two exploratory solutions, the fit indices and standardised loadings of the three confirmatory models, and the reliability table. The numbers of sections 10 and 11 come from files written by the course pipeline into `data/`: the counts of the respondents who mention nothing and the cell means under each rule (`teney_panel_weights.csv` and `teney_panel_measurement.csv`, by `R/07_measurement_panels.R`), the imputations, run with the mice and Amelia packages (`spec_grid_mi.csv` and `mi_diagnostics.csv`, by `08_mi_tier.R`), and the curve with the comparison of each option with its twins (`spec_curve.csv`, `menu_deviations.csv` and `menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz`, by `09_spec_curve.R` and `11_menu_deviations.R`). The respondent-level file is never distributed with the course, and the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) explains the registration route to the raw data.
